name: Random Sequence Generator Calculator
seoTitle: Random Sequence Generator Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: Generate a random DNA, RNA or protein sequence of any length with a target GC content, and get the same sequence back every time from the same seed. Free rand
summary:
Generate a random DNA, RNA or protein sequence of any length with a target GC content, and get the same sequence back every time from the same seed. It returns gc content of the output, and the panel shows all of them at once.

It is the negative control you need for a motif search, a composition baseline for a GC calculator, or a training example for a pipeline. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.html:

sections.title: How do I use the Random Sequence Generator?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Choose the alphabet, the length and — for DNA or RNA — the GC content you want.
  2. Keep the seed if you need the same sequence again, change it for a different draw.
  3. Copy the output: it is wrapped at 60 columns and the seed is printed with it, so anyone can reproduce exactly what you used.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: length of 1,000 residues, target gc content of 50%, seed of 42, make the sequence start with atg of 0.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
20 – 40 % GCAT-richtypical of a bacterial genome's variable regions and of some promoters
40 – 60 % GCBalancedthe usual null model for a mammalian sequence
60 – 80 % GCGC-richlike a CpG island or a GC3-rich coding sequence

  • The random draw is deterministic from the seed: the same seed and length always give the same sequence, which is what makes a 'random' control reproducible in a paper.

  • GC is applied as a target, so the achieved value wobbles around it by the binomial sampling error — for 1 000 bases at 50 %, expect about ±1.6 points.

  • A protein draw uses the 20 standard residues with equal probability, not the natural amino-acid frequencies; that is what you want for a shuffled control, and it is stated in the output rather than assumed.

  • Nothing here is cryptographically random. For keys or identifiers use a proper CSPRNG.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Using a random sequence as a statistical null without matching its GC content to the real sequence — composition dominates most motif statistics.
  • Assuming two different seeds give unrelated sequences: they do, but a short sequence can happen to look similar, which is the point of the test.
  • Generating a 'random' protein with natural frequencies and calling it a shuffled control.
  • Losing the seed and then being unable to reproduce a figure.

faq.a: It is pseudo-random and deterministic from the seed: statistically uniform, perfectly reproducible, and not suitable for anything security-related.

faq.q: Why does the GC content not exactly match what I asked for?
faq.a: Because each base is drawn independently, so the realised count fluctuates around the target — more bases means a smaller wobble. The page reports what it actually produced.

faq.q: Can I regenerate the same sequence later?
faq.a: Yes — keep the seed and the length. The output block prints the seed for exactly that reason.

faq.q: Does the protein mode use natural amino-acid frequencies?
faq.a: No. It draws the 20 residues uniformly, which is the right control for a shuffled sequence. Use a composition-matched generator if your null model needs natural frequencies.

faq.q: What does the Random Sequence Generator actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns gc content of the output. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.
